items.rationale: The difference between a workflow and an agent is who decides the next step. In c the model chooses each next call and when to stop, so the model owns the control flow. In a, b and d the program's code fixes the sequence and the model only does a task inside it, even in a, where the model picks a label but the code decides what happens next. Picking any of those shows the belief that using a model in a pipeline already makes it an agent.

The script's code fixes the order (extract, describe, check) and decides when the run ends, so the code owns the control flow and this is a workflow. A model doing each step does not change that. Counting the model calls (b), passing outputs forward (c) or having a model carry out every step (d) does not make an agent: an agent is defined by the model choosing the next step, and here the code does.

The three steps are known in advance and are the same for every booking request, so the code can fix the order and nothing needs the model to choose. A fixed workflow is cheaper and more predictable here. Answering agent shows the belief that an agent is always the better, more capable choice (M8), even when its flexibility goes unused.

Extra calls per request = 7 - 3 = 4 calls. Extra cost per request = 4 calls x $0.002 = $0.008. Over 1,000 requests: $0.008 x 1,000 = $8 saved, with the same result, because the extra calls add nothing. Answering 14 (the agent's total, 7 x 0.002 x 1,000) or 6 (the workflow's total) gives a total instead of the difference.

A fixed workflow fits when the steps are known in advance and the same every time, which is true of reading, labeling and recording each email. In a, c and d the next action depends on what was just found, so the number and order of steps cannot be fixed beforehand and an agent's flexibility is needed. Choosing one of those shows the belief that an agent is always the more capable, better choice, even where its flexibility goes unused and it costs more.

The steps are always the same four, so the agent's freedom to choose is unused: it costs 9 calls instead of a few, and a missed email is what one would expect when the model chooses each step, since nothing forces it to do the last one. Code that runs the steps in a fixed order always reaches the email step and calls the model only where one is needed, so it fixes both problems. More steps (a), a larger model (b) or more tools (c) add agent power to a task that needs none, and none of them forces the email step to run; this is the belief that agents are the answer to every problem.
